name: Nkala
body:
NKALA
CR 4

This large red crab is several feet across, its spiny carapace covered in strange whorls and patterns. It has strange beak-like heads at both the front and back of its body.

XP 1,200
N Medium aberration
Init +6; Senses darkvision 60 ft., see invisibility; Perception +11

DEFENSE

AC 17, touch 12, flat-footed 15 (+2 Dex, +5 natural)
hp 38 (7d8+7)
Fort +5, Ref +4, Will +6; +4 vs. blinding and visual effects
Defensive Abilities all-around vision, dual faces

OFFENSE

Speed 30 ft., swim 20 ft.
Melee 2 claws +8 (1d6+2 plus shadow steal)
Special Attacks consume shadow, shadow steal

STATISTICS

Str 15, Dex 14, Con 13, Int 6, Wis 13, Cha 8
Base Atk +5; CMB +7; CMD 19
Feats Ability Focus (shadow steal), Great Fortitude, Improved Initiative, Weapon Focus (claws)
Skills Perception +11, Stealth +12, Swim +10
Languages one language of its former summoner (can’t speak)
SQ amphibious

SPECIAL ABILITIES

Consume Shadow (Su)

When a nkala critically hits with its claw or a target fails its save against the nkala’s shadow steal ability, as a swift action it devours a portion of the target’s shadow and gains 2d4 temporary hit points, which last for 1 minute or until expended.

Dual Faces (Ex)

A nkala’s two heads grant them a +4 bonus on saving throws against visual effects, including being blinded or dazzled. If it fails a save and would be blinded, it is not blinded but instead loses this saving throw bonus as well as its all-around vision and see invisibility abilities for as long as that effect lasts.

If affected by another effect that causes blindness, the nkala is blinded.

Shadow Steal (Su)

A creature struck by the nkala’s claw is fatigued (DC 16 Fort negates), as the creature leaches away at its vitality through its shadow. If the target is already fatigued and fails a save, it contracts a supernatural wasting sickness called shadow blight.

Shadow blight: Bite—injury; save Fort DC 14; onset 1 day; frequency 1/day; effect 1d2 Str damage and 1d2 Cha damage; cure 2 consecutive saves. The save DC is Constitution-based.

ECOLOGY

Environment warm rivers and coastlines
Organization solitary
Treasure none

Among riverside villages and oceanside beach settlements, tales are still whispered of the nkala—a strange creature feared not for its claws, but for its unusual hunger.

Resembling a massive crab nearly the size of a person, the nkala’s possesses two faces: one at the front of its shell and another on its back, each with the general appearance like that of a hippopotamus. Both seem to move and blink independently, giving the impression that the creature sees in every direction at once. Locals say one face watches the living world, while the other sees into the realm of spirits.

Despite its bulk, the nkala is a quiet predator. It moves with surprising grace along muddy riverbanks and coastal shallows, leaving few signs of its passing. What makes it truly feared, however, is not its strength or speed, but its appetite.

The nkala does not consume flesh or bone—it feeds on shadows. Victims struck by its claws sometimes survive the encounter, only to find themselves hollowed out, numb to joy or sorrow, unable to dream or recall their own past clearly. Some claim the creature strips away something essential, leaving behind a body with no soul.

Though feared in the wild, the nkala are sometimes found as wizard familiars. Such an unusual choice is always noteworthy, for the nkala chooses its master as much as it is chosen, and it demands offerings of shadow to maintain its loyalty. Some say those who keep a nkala too long begin to mirror its habits—watching the world with two faces and dreaming of places not meant for mortal minds.

Even in death, the nkala is treated with caution. Its claws are burned or buried beneath flowing water, and people avoid looking directly at the faces for fear of acquiring some lingering curse. Yet, for all the fear it inspires, the nkala is not seen as wholly evil. Some believe it was once a guardian spirit twisted by misuse of magic, or a creature tasked with keeping balance between the seen and unseen. Whether a punishment or protector, the nkala endures in the stories people pass down.
